title: Introduction to Chemical Reactions & Observations
description: Master the identification of chemical reactions through everyday observations, word equations, and skeletal chemical equations.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 1: Introduction to Chemical Reactions & Observations. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Emphasize real-life examples like souring of milk or rusting of iron to ground the concept.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: A spirit lamp, tongs holding Mg ribbon, watch-glass collecting white ash.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Chemical Reactions -> Observations (Gas, Temp, Colour, State) -> Word Equations -> Skeletal Equations
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Chemical Reactions -> Observations (Gas, Temp, Colour, State) -> Word Equations -> Skeletal Equations") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Chemical Reaction: "A process in which substances undergo a chemical change to form new substances with entirely different properties." [SI Unit: N/A]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Magnesium Ribbon Burning: Burning a cleaned magnesium ribbon in air producing a dazzling white flame and white powder of magnesium oxide.

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Page 2:
    * [Q1] (conceptual): Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning in air?
      Method: Magnesium reacts with moist air to form a protective layer of magnesium oxide on its surface. Rubbing with sandpaper removes this layer so pure magnesium can burn.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Chemical Reaction":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): Which of the following is not a characteristic of a chemical reaction?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Change in mass
      -> Socratic Hint: Recall the law of conservation of mass; mass remains constant.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): State two observations that indicate a chemical reaction has taken place.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Evolution of a gas and change in temperature.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about what happens when zinc reacts with dilute acid.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Chemical Reaction":
    - Visual Title: "Magnesium Combustion" (vector_svg_diagram)
    - Why Needed: Visualizes Activity 1.1 clearly.
    - What to Explain: Explain how magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame.
    - Timing & Directive: Introduce at start of class.

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
success_criteria: Identify and write correct word and skeletal equations for given chemical changes.
chapter_notes: A chemical reaction involves the breaking and making of bonds between atoms to produce new substances. The initial substances are reactants and new substances are products. Observations include change in state, colour, evolution of gas, and change in temperature.

worked_examples.given: Reactants: Magnesium and Oxygen; Product: Magnesium oxide
worked_examples.problem: Write the word equation for burning of magnesium in air.
worked_examples.calculation: Combine reactants on LHS and product on RHS with an arrow.

common_misconceptions: Confusing physical changes with chemical changes.

title: Balancing Chemical Equations & Physical States
description: Learn the law of conservation of mass and master the step-by-step hit-and-trial method for balancing chemical equations.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 2: Balancing Chemical Equations & Physical States. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Walk through the 7 steps of balancing the iron-water reaction meticulously.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Comparison table for atom balancing.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Unbalanced Equation -> Draw Boxes -> Count Atoms -> Max Atom Rule (Hit & Trial) -> Add States (s,l,g,aq)
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Unbalanced Equation -> Draw Boxes -> Count Atoms -> Max Atom Rule (Hit & Trial) -> Add States (s,l,g,aq)") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Balanced Chemical Equation: "An equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both the reactant and product sides." [SI Unit: N/A]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Balancing Iron and Steam Reaction: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Page 6:
    * [Q2] (numerical): Write the balanced equation for Hydrogen + Chlorine -> Hydrogen chloride
      Method: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Law of Conservation of Mass":
    * [Q1] (2-mark Definition): Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: To satisfy the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about atomic mass conservation on LHS and RHS.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Hit-and-Trial Method":
    - Visual Title: "Atom Count Table" (vector_svg_diagram)
    - Why Needed: Helps students systematically check atom balance.
    - What to Explain: Compare element counts on LHS and RHS.
    - Timing & Directive: Use during equation balancing.

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
success_criteria: Successfully balance complex skeletal equations such as Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2.
subtopics: Incorporating Physical States (s, l, g, aq)
chapter_notes: Mass can neither be created nor destroyed. Therefore, the total number of atoms of each element must be equal on both LHS and RHS of a chemical equation. We use the hit-and-trial method starting from the compound with maximum atoms.

worked_examples.calculation: Atoms on both sides are equal.

common_misconceptions: Altering formulas inside the boxes (e.g., changing H2O to H2O2) instead of changing coefficients.

title: Types of Reactions: Combination & Decomposition
description: Understand combination and thermal, electrolytic, and photolytic decomposition reactions with accompanying energy changes.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 3: Types of Reactions: Combination & Decomposition. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Highlight electrolysis of water (Activity 1.7) and silver chloride photolysis (Activity 1.8).
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Plastic mug with carbon electrodes and inverted test tubes.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Reaction Types -> Combination (A+B -> C) | Decomposition (A -> B+C) [Thermal, Electrolytic, Photolytic]
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Reaction Types -> Combination (A+B -> C) | Decomposition (A -> B+C) [Thermal, Electrolytic, Photolytic]") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Decomposition Reaction: "A reaction in which a single reactant breaks down to give two or more simpler products." [SI Unit: N/A]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Slaked Lime Formation: CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Page 10:
    * [Q1] (conceptual): A solution of a substance 'X' is used for whitewashing. (i) Name 'X' and its formula. (ii) Write the reaction with water.
      Method: (i) Calcium oxide, CaO. (ii) CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Combination Reaction":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): Which of the following is a combination reaction? (A) CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (B) CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (A)
      -> Socratic Hint: Combination means two or more reactants forming a single product.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Electrolytic Decomposition":
    - Visual Title: "Water Electrolysis" (vector_svg_diagram)
    - Why Needed: Shows 2:1 ratio of H2 and O2 gases.
    - What to Explain: Explain why hydrogen gas volume is double of oxygen.
    - Timing & Directive: Discuss during Activity 1.7.

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
success_criteria: Differentiate between combination and decomposition reactions and classify energy requirements.
chapter_notes: Combination reactions involve two or more substances combining to form a single product. Decomposition reactions are the exact opposite, where a single reactant breaks down into simpler products using heat, light, or electricity.

worked_examples.given: Single reactant breaking down into multiple products with heat.
worked_examples.problem: Identify the type of reaction: 2FeSO4(s) -> Fe2O3(s) + SO2(g) + SO3(g)

common_misconceptions: Confusing endothermic processes with exothermic ones.

text.explanation: Types of Reactions: Combination & Decomposition: Understand combination and thermal, electrolytic, and photolytic decomposition reactions with accompanying energy changes.

title: Displacement & Double Displacement Reactions
description: Master displacement and double displacement reactions, reactivity series, and precipitation processes.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 4: Displacement & Double Displacement Reactions. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Use the reactivity series to explain why iron displaces copper but copper cannot displace iron.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Test tube with blue CuSO4 solution and iron nail.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Reaction Types -> Displacement (A + BC -> AC + B) | Double Displacement (AB + CD -> AD + CB)
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Reaction Types -> Displacement (A + BC -> AC + B) | Double Displacement (AB + CD -> AD + CB)") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Precipitation Reaction: "Any reaction that produces an insoluble substance (precipitate)." [SI Unit: N/A]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Iron Nail in Copper Sulphate: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Page 13:
    * [Q2] (conceptual): Give an example of a double displacement reaction other than Activity 1.10.
      Method: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Displacement Reaction":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): What happens when iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Iron displaces copper, turning solution light green and nail brownish.
      -> Socratic Hint: Iron is more reactive than copper.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Displacement Reaction":
    - Visual Title: "Iron & Copper Sulphate" (vector_svg_diagram)
    - Why Needed: Visualizes color change from blue to green.
    - What to Explain: Explain how Fe displaces Cu.
    - Timing & Directive: Discuss during Activity 1.9.

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
success_criteria: Predict whether a displacement reaction will occur based on the reactivity series and write ionic exchange equations.
chapter_notes: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. In double displacement reactions, two ionic species exchange partners, often forming an insoluble precipitate.

worked_examples.problem: Write the balanced equation for sodium sulphate and barium chloride reaction.

common_misconceptions: Assuming less reactive metals can displace more reactive metals.

title: Oxidation, Reduction, Corrosion & Rancidity
description: Master oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions and understand everyday consequences like corrosion and rancidity.
ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 5: Oxidation, Reduction, Corrosion & Rancidity. Mid-Term Examination Syllabus. Use clear arrows to show electron/oxygen transfer during redox reactions on the board.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: Tripod stand, wire gauze, china dish with copper powder, and burner.
- Diagram Type: vector_svg_diagram
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Redox -> Oxidation (Gain O / Lose H) + Reduction (Lose O / Gain H) -> Everyday Effects (Corrosion, Rancidity)
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Redox -> Oxidation (Gain O / Lose H) + Reduction (Lose O / Gain H) -> Everyday Effects (Corrosion, Rancidity)") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Redox Reaction: "A chemical reaction in which one reactant gets oxidised while the other gets reduced." [SI Unit: N/A]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Copper to Copper Oxide: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO (Heating copper powder)

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Page 13:
    * [Q3] (conceptual): Identify substances oxidised and reduced in: CuO(s) + H2(g) -> Cu(s) + H2O(l)
      Method: H2 is oxidised to H2O; CuO is reduced to Cu.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Oxidation and Reduction":
    * [Q1] (2-mark Definition): Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen transfer.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen; reduction is the loss of oxygen.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about copper turning to copper oxide.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Redox Reaction":
    - Visual Title: "Oxidation & Reduction Flow" (vector_svg_diagram)
    - Why Needed: Clearly distinguishes oxidation vs reduction.
    - What to Explain: Trace oxygen gain and loss.
    - Timing & Directive: Use when explaining redox definitions.

- MANDATORY WHITEBOARD INSTRUCTION: Each concept in this capsule has a DISTINCT, dedicated visual. You MUST call render_svg_diagram or draw_graph with that concept's UNIQUE diagram when teaching it! NEVER duplicate or reuse the same diagram across different concepts!
- STRICT SOCRATIC PROGRESSION GATING: After teaching each concept in small bites of 2-3 sentences, you MUST pose at least one of the prepared 4-6 exam questions above to the student. You MUST strictly wait for the student to answer or explicitly ask for the answer before advancing to the next concept! Never lecture continuously without student response.
- EXPLANATION MANDATE: When explaining definitions, formulas, and algebraic transitions, unpack the physical meaning and the "why" behind each line out loud. Never merely recite the text!
success_criteria: Identify oxidizing and reducing agents in given redox equations and explain corrosion prevention.
subtopics: Oxidation Definition (Gain of Oxygen / Loss of Hydrogen)
Reduction Definition (Loss of Oxygen / Gain of Hydrogen)
chapter_notes: If a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen during a reaction, it is oxidised. If it loses oxygen or gains hydrogen, it is reduced. Reactions where both occur simultaneously are redox reactions. Corrosion and rancidity are everyday oxidative degradation processes.

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 1.1, p. 6): Why must a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning in air?
worked_examples.given: Magnesium ribbon stored in laboratory environment.
worked_examples.substitution: Magnesium reacts with atmospheric oxygen over time to form a protective layer of basic magnesium oxide.
worked_examples.calculation: The layer of basic magnesium oxide prevents contact between magnesium metal and atmospheric oxygen. Rubbing with sandpaper removes this inert coating so that clean magnesium can ignite readily.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Cleaned to remove the inert magnesium oxide protective coating so the metal can ignite.

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 1.1, p. 6): Write balanced chemical equations for: (a) Hydrogen + Chlorine -> Hydrogen chloride, (b) Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate -> Barium sulphate + Aluminium chloride, (c) Sodium + Water -> Sodium hydroxide + Hydrogen.
worked_examples.given: Three word equations for chemical reactions.
worked_examples.formula: Law of Conservation of Mass; balancing coefficients.
worked_examples.substitution: Equate atoms on reactant and product sides.

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 1.2, p. 10): A solution of substance 'X' is used for whitewashing. (a) Name substance 'X' and state its formula. (b) Write the reaction of 'X' with water. (c) Why does lime water turn milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled through?
worked_examples.given: Whitewashing chemistry; reaction with water and atmospheric CO2.
worked_examples.formula: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (Slaking of lime); Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O.
worked_examples.substitution: Calcium oxide (quicklime) dissolves exothermically in water.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Substance X is Quicklime; chemical formula is CaO (Calcium oxide).
(b) CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + Heat (Slaked lime).
(c) Passing CO2 through clear lime water Ca(OH)2 forms insoluble calcium carbonate precipitate (CaCO3), which creates the milky turbidity.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Substance X is CaO (Quicklime); (b) CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + Heat; (c) Insoluble CaCO3 precipitate causes milkiness.
worked_examples.image_search_query: quicklime slaked lime calcium carbonate whitewash

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 1.2, p. 10): Why is the volume of gas collected at one electrode during electrolysis of water double that of the other? Name both gases.
worked_examples.substitution: At cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2; At anode: 2O(2-) -> O2 + 4e-.
worked_examples.calculation: Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Decomposition releases two molecules of hydrogen gas for every one molecule of oxygen gas. Per Avogadro's law, equal moles of gases occupy equal volumes, so hydrogen volume is double oxygen volume.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Hydrogen gas at the cathode is double the volume of oxygen gas at the anode (2 : 1 volume ratio).
worked_examples.figure_caption: Water electrolysis apparatus showing 2:1 gas volume ratio
worked_examples.image_search_query: electrolysis of water apparatus cathode anode gases

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 1.2, p. 13): Why does the blue colour of copper sulphate solution fade and change to light green when an iron nail is dipped in it?
worked_examples.given: Iron nail placed in aqueous CuSO4 solution.
worked_examples.formula: Single displacement reaction: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s).
worked_examples.substitution: Iron is more reactive than copper in the activity series.
worked_examples.calculation: Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution because Fe is higher in the reactivity series than Cu. The blue Cu2+ ions are reduced to reddish-brown copper metal deposited on the nail, while green Fe2+ (ferrous sulphate) ions enter solution.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Iron displaces copper to form light green ferrous sulphate (FeSO4) while reddish-brown copper deposits on the nail.
worked_examples.figure_caption: Iron nail in copper sulphate solution single displacement
worked_examples.image_search_query: iron nail in copper sulphate solution displacement

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q4 & Q5 (p. 15): (a) What is a balanced chemical equation and why must equations be balanced? (b) Translate into balanced equations: Nitrogen gas combines with hydrogen gas to form ammonia; Hydrogen sulphide gas burns in air to give water and sulphur dioxide.
worked_examples.given: Law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions.
worked_examples.formula: Sum of reactant atoms = Sum of product atoms; N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3; 2H2S + 3O2 -> 2H2O + 2SO2.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) An equation where the total number of atoms of each element on reactant side equals the product side. Per the Law of Conservation of Mass, matter cannot be created or destroyed.
(b) Nitrogen + Hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g).
(c) Hydrogen sulphide in air: 2H2S(g) + 3O2(g) -> 2H2O(l) + 2SO2(g).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Must be balanced to satisfy the Law of Conservation of Mass; (b) N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3; (c) 2H2S + 3O2 -> 2H2O + 2SO2.
worked_examples.image_search_query: chemical reaction mass conservation balanced equation

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q6, Q7, Q8 (p. 15): Balance: (a) HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + H2O, (b) NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O, (c) BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + HCl, (d) Zn + 2AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) 2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O
(b) 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O
(c) BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl
(d) Zn + 2AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag (Displacement reaction)
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) 2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O; (b) 2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O; (c) BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl; (d) Zn + 2AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag.
worked_examples.image_search_query: balanced chemical equations ncert class 10 solutions

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q9 & Q10 (p. 15): (a) Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions with equations. (b) Why is cellular respiration considered an exothermic reaction?
worked_examples.given: Enthalpy and energy flow in chemical processes.
worked_examples.formula: Exothermic: Reactants -> Products + Energy; Endothermic: Reactants + Energy -> Products.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Exothermic reactions release thermal/chemical energy to surroundings (e.g. burning methane: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + Heat). Endothermic reactions absorb thermal energy (e.g. CaCO3 + Heat -> CaO + CO2).
(b) In cellular respiration, glucose is oxidised by inhaled oxygen in mitochondria, releasing 2870 kJ/mol of energy trapped as ATP for cellular work. Because energy is liberated, respiration is exothermic.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Exothermic releases heat while endothermic absorbs heat; (b) Respiration oxidises glucose, releasing energy as ATP, making it exothermic.
worked_examples.image_search_query: exothermic vs endothermic reactions respiration chemistry

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q16 & Q17 (p. 16): (a) Explain Oxidation and Reduction in terms of oxygen gain/loss. (b) A shiny brown element 'X' on heating in air turns black. Identify 'X' and the black compound.
worked_examples.given: Redox principles; thermal oxidation of element X.
worked_examples.formula: Oxidation: Gain of oxygen; Reduction: Loss of oxygen. 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO.
worked_examples.substitution: Element X is Copper (Cu); black compound is Copper(II) oxide (CuO).
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Oxidation involves gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen (e.g., 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO). Reduction involves loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen (e.g., CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O).
(b) Shiny brown element X is Copper metal (Cu). When heated in air, it reacts with oxygen to form a black surface coating of Copper(II) oxide: 2Cu(s) + O2(g) -> 2CuO(s).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Oxidation = gain of oxygen, Reduction = loss of oxygen; (b) Element X is Copper (Cu), black substance is Copper(II) oxide (CuO).
worked_examples.image_search_query: copper oxidation black copper oxide heating air

worked_examples.problem: End-of-Chapter Exercise Q18 & Q19 (p. 16): (a) Why do we apply paint on iron articles? (b) Why are oil and fat containing food items flushed with nitrogen gas?
worked_examples.given: Prevention of corrosion and food rancidity.
worked_examples.formula: Rusting requires Fe + O2 + H2O; Rancidity is aerobic oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids.
worked_examples.substitution: Barrier protection and inert gas atmosphere.
worked_examples.calculation:
(a) Paint forms an impermeable barrier preventing atmospheric oxygen and moisture from contacting the surface of iron, preventing rust (hydrated ferric oxide Fe2O3.xH2O) formation.
(b) Oils and fats undergo oxidation when exposed to air, producing volatile foul-smelling aldehydes and ketones (rancidity). Flushing with unreactive nitrogen gas expels oxygen, preventing oxidation and preserving food freshness.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Paint blocks oxygen and moisture to stop rust; (b) Nitrogen gas is inert and displaces oxygen to prevent oxidative rancidity.
worked_examples.image_search_query: corrosion prevention painting food packaging nitrogen rancidity

common_misconceptions: Forgetting to balance polyatomic ions as single units when convenient.
